questions.question: What is an Auto Scaling Group and why do we use it?
questions.answer: An Auto Scaling Group (ASG) is an AWS service that automatically manages a fleet of EC2 instances. It adds instances when demand increases (scale out) and removes them when demand drops (scale in). We use it to achieve high availability (auto-replacement of failed instances), cost efficiency (only pay for what you need), and elasticity (handle traffic spikes automatically without manual intervention).

questions.question: What are the three things you must configure when creating an Auto Scaling Group?
questions.answer: 1. Launch Template — defines what kind of EC2 instance to launch (AMI, instance type, security groups, key pair, user data). 2. Size Limits — Minimum (never go below), Desired (target count), Maximum (never exceed). 3. Scaling Policy — defines the conditions that trigger scaling actions (when and how to scale).

questions.question: What is the difference between Minimum Size, Desired Capacity, and Maximum Size in ASG?
questions.answer: Minimum Size: ASG never scales below this, even during zero traffic — ensures baseline availability. Desired Capacity: the target number ASG tries to maintain at all times — it starts with this count. Maximum Size: ASG never creates more than this, even during peak traffic — caps cost and capacity.

questions.question: What is a Launch Template and why is it required by ASG?
questions.answer: A Launch Template is a reusable configuration blueprint for EC2 instances — it contains the AMI, instance type, key pair, security groups, and user data. ASG needs it because when scaling out, it must create new identical instances. Without a blueprint, it wouldn't know what to launch. Think of it as a franchise manual — every new branch is built the same way.

questions.question: What is Target Tracking Scaling and why does AWS recommend it?
questions.answer: Target Tracking Scaling automatically adjusts the number of instances to keep a specific metric (e.g., CPU utilization) at a target value you set. AWS recommends it because it's the simplest to configure (no alarm thresholds to define) and most intelligent in response — it continuously calculates the optimal instance count like a thermostat maintains room temperature.

questions.question: What is the difference between Step Scaling and Simple Scaling?
questions.answer: Step Scaling defines multiple scaling actions based on how much a metric exceeds a threshold — the response is proportional to the severity. (e.g., CPU 60% → add 1; CPU 80% → add 2; CPU 90% → add 3). Simple Scaling performs one fixed action when an alarm fires, then waits for a cooldown period before any further action. Step Scaling is more responsive; Simple Scaling can lag during sustained traffic spikes.

questions.question: When would you use Scheduled Scaling versus Predictive Scaling?
questions.answer: Scheduled Scaling: when you know exactly when traffic will increase — planned events, batch jobs at fixed times, business hours. (e.g., every Monday 9 AM add 5 instances). Predictive Scaling: when traffic patterns are recurring but you want the ML algorithm to discover and act on them automatically. Best for weekly/daily cycles with 2+ weeks of history. Scheduled is explicit; Predictive is automatic pattern detection.

questions.question: What is an Application Load Balancer and at which OSI layer does it operate?
questions.answer: An Application Load Balancer (ALB) is a managed AWS service that distributes incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic across multiple targets (EC2 instances, Lambda, containers). It operates at Layer 7 (Application Layer) of the OSI model, which means it can read the content of HTTP requests — enabling path-based routing, host-based routing, and header-based routing decisions.

questions.question: What are the core components of an ALB and how do they relate to each other?
questions.answer: Three core components: 1. Listener — sits on a port/protocol (e.g., port 80 HTTP), waits for incoming connections, applies rules. 2. Rules — conditions and actions on the Listener; when a request matches a condition, it's forwarded to the appropriate Target Group. 3. Target Group — the destination; holds EC2 instances (or Lambda/IPs), manages health checks, receives forwarded traffic. Flow: User → ALB Listener → Rules evaluated → Matching Target Group → Healthy Target.

questions.question: What is the difference between path-based routing and host-based routing in ALB?
questions.answer: Path-based routing routes based on the URL path in the request. e.g., /api/* → API servers, /images/* → media servers. Host-based routing routes based on the domain name (Host header). e.g., api.company.com → API Target Group, www.company.com → Web Target Group. Both can be combined in the same ALB rules. Path-based handles microservices under one domain; host-based handles multiple subdomains on one ALB.

questions.question: Situation: Your EC2 instance passes all EC2 status checks, but the application on it is returning 500 errors. Users are still hitting that instance. How do you fix this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Instance appears healthy at OS level but application is broken. (Task) Ensure users aren't routed to broken instances. (Action) Enable ELB health checks on the ASG (not just EC2 health checks). ELB health checks test at the application level — they send HTTP requests and check for 2xx/3xx responses. If the app returns 500, ALB marks the instance unhealthy and removes it from rotation. ASG then terminates and replaces it. (Result) Users are only ever routed to healthy instances at the application level.

questions.question: Situation: Your startup's website traffic spikes every Friday at 5 PM for 3 hours. The rest of the week is quiet. How do you set up cost-efficient auto scaling?
questions.answer: (Situation) Predictable weekly spike on Friday evenings. (Task) Handle the spike without over-provisioning all week. (Action) Use Scheduled Scaling — create a schedule to scale up to 8 instances at 4:45 PM every Friday (before the spike), and scale back down to 2 instances at 8 PM. Combine with a baseline Target Tracking policy for unexpected spikes during off-peak hours. Set Minimum=2 (cost control), Desired=2 (normal), Maximum=8 (spike capacity). (Result) You only pay for extra instances during the 3-hour peak window.

questions.question: Situation: A developer cannot access EC2 instances behind an ALB via their browser. The ALB DNS works fine. The instances are healthy in the Target Group. What's the likely issue?
questions.answer: (Situation) ALB works but direct access fails — or ALB shows no response. (Task) Diagnose and fix. (Action) Most likely the EC2 security group allows inbound traffic only from the ALB's security group (as per best practice), not from 0.0.0.0/0. This is correct — users should only access instances through the ALB. If the developer is trying to hit the instance's public IP directly, they shouldn't be. If the issue is that the ALB itself isn't responding: check the ALB security group allows port 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0, and check the listener is configured correctly. (Result) Fix the appropriate security group based on actual root cause.

questions.question: Situation: You're deploying a new version of your application with zero downtime. Your existing instances are in a Blue Target Group. How do you do this with ALB?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need zero-downtime deployment. (Task) Release new version without interrupting users. (Action) Blue/Green deployment: Create a Green Target Group with new instances running the new version. Point both Blue and Green Target Groups to the same ALB listener. Start by sending 90% traffic to Blue (existing), 10% to Green (weighted routing). Monitor error rates and latency on Green. If healthy, gradually shift: 50/50, then 10/90, then 0/100. (Result) Zero downtime — if Green has issues, instantly switch back to 100% Blue. Once validated, delete Blue instances to save cost.

questions.question: Situation: Your ASG keeps launching and terminating the same instance repeatedly in a loop. What could cause this?
questions.answer: (Situation) ASG in a scaling loop — creating and immediately destroying instances. (Task) Diagnose and stop the loop. (Action) This is called a 'flapping' issue. Common causes: 1. Health check grace period too short — instances terminate before the app finishes starting up. Fix: increase the health check grace period. 2. Health check misconfigured — wrong path, wrong port. Fix: check the Target Group health check path returns 200. 3. User data script failing — instances launch but the app never starts. Fix: check CloudWatch logs / instance logs. (Result) After identifying root cause, fix configuration and the loop stops.

questions.question: Situation: A company runs an e-commerce site and wants requests for /shop/* to go to the product servers and /checkout/* to go to the payment servers. What ALB setup achieves this?
questions.answer: (Situation) URL-based routing needed for different backends. (Task) Route two paths to two different server groups. (Action) Create two Target Groups — TG-Products and TG-Payments. On the ALB listener (port 443): Rule 1 (priority 1): Condition: Path is /shop/* → Action: Forward to TG-Products. Rule 2 (priority 2): Condition: Path is /checkout/* → Action: Forward to TG-Payments. Default Rule: Forward remaining traffic to TG-Products (or a general group). (Result) Users visiting /shop URLs hit product servers; /checkout URLs hit payment servers — all behind one domain and one ALB.

questions.question: Situation: Your ASG scaled out from 3 to 6 instances during a peak. The peak is over. Traffic dropped back to normal but instances are still at 6. What's happening?
questions.answer: (Situation) Scale-in not triggering as expected. (Task) Understand why ASG isn't scaling in. (Action) Check: 1. Cooldown period — ASG waits for the cooldown to expire (default 300s) before scaling in. 2. Scale-in protection — some instances may have scale-in protection enabled. 3. Target Tracking — it scales in conservatively to avoid oscillation. By design, it's slower to scale in than scale out. 4. Minimum size — if you're already at Minimum, no further scale-in happens. Give it time — Target Tracking typically scales in over several minutes, not immediately. (Result) If none apply, check if the metric has actually dropped below the target and that the warmup period has passed.

questions.question: Situation: You need to add a security appliance (like a firewall) in line with all traffic entering your VPC. Which load balancer type handles this?
questions.answer: (Situation) Need third-party security appliance (firewall, IDS/IPS) inline with traffic. (Task) Route all traffic through the appliance before it reaches the app. (Action) Use Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB). GWLB operates at Layer 3, intercepts all IP traffic, and distributes it to a fleet of security appliances (registered in a Target Group). After inspection, traffic is forwarded to the actual destination. This is the only load balancer designed for this use case. ALB and NLB are for application-level load balancing, not traffic inspection. (Result) GWLB ensures 100% of traffic is inspected by your security appliance fleet.

questions.question: Situation: A company wants to deploy their app in 3 AZs for maximum fault tolerance with an ASG. What's the minimum configuration needed?
questions.answer: (Situation) High availability across 3 AZs. (Task) Design ASG + ALB for 3-AZ fault tolerance. (Action) 1. Create one subnet per AZ (3 total) in your VPC. 2. ASG: Select all 3 subnets — ASG distributes instances across AZs automatically. Set Minimum=3 (one per AZ), Desired=3, Maximum=6. 3. ALB: Enable all 3 AZs (map to each subnet). Cross-Zone Load Balancing (default on ALB) ensures even traffic distribution. 4. If one AZ goes down, ASG relaunches in remaining AZs; ALB stops routing to unhealthy AZ. (Result) App remains available even if one entire AZ fails.

questions.question: Situation: Your app processes images at /api/process and serves static files from /static. The image processing is CPU-intensive and needs large instances; static files are lightweight. How do you optimize cost?
questions.answer: (Situation) Two endpoints with very different resource needs. (Task) Right-size instances for each workload. (Action) Create two ASGs: ASG-1 (c5.2xlarge instances, for CPU work) with Target Group TG-Process. ASG-2 (t3.small instances, for static files) with Target Group TG-Static. ALB Listener Rules: /api/process/* → TG-Process; /static/* → TG-Static. Each ASG can scale independently based on its workload — no need to use expensive instances for static file serving. (Result) Significant cost savings — right-sized infrastructure per workload type, independently scalable.

questions.question: Compare ALB and NLB. In what scenarios would you choose each?
questions.answer: ALB (Application Load Balancer - Layer 7): Choose when you need HTTP/HTTPS routing, path-based or host-based routing, WebSocket support, integration with WAF, or Lambda as a target. Best for web applications and microservices. NLB (Network Load Balancer - Layer 4): Choose when you need ultra-high performance (millions of requests/second), static IP addresses for the load balancer, TCP/UDP protocol support, very low latency (<1ms), or TLS passthrough. Best for gaming, IoT, financial apps requiring extreme performance. Rule of thumb: Web app = ALB. High-performance TCP/UDP = NLB.

questions.question: How does the ASG Lifecycle work when scaling out and scaling in?
questions.answer: Scale-Out Lifecycle: 1. ASG determines more capacity is needed (policy triggered). 2. ASG launches instance using Launch Template. 3. Instance enters 'Pending' state → 'Pending:Wait' (lifecycle hooks, if any). 4. Instance enters 'InService' — ASG registers it with Target Group. 5. ALB starts health checks; after passing, traffic flows. Scale-In Lifecycle: 1. ASG determines excess capacity. 2. Instance selected for termination (default policy: oldest launch config, or farthest from billing hour). 3. Instance enters 'Terminating' → 'Terminating:Wait' (connection draining on ALB). 4. After drain delay, deregistered from Target Group. 5. Instance terminated. 6. State = 'Terminated'.

questions.question: What is the ASG Default Termination Policy and how does it work?
questions.answer: When ASG needs to scale in, it uses the Default Termination Policy to choose which instance to remove: 1. It selects the AZ with the most instances first (to balance AZs). 2. Within that AZ, it terminates the instance using the oldest launch configuration/template. 3. If tied, it terminates the instance closest to the next billing hour (to save cost). You can override this with custom termination policies: OldestInstance, NewestInstance, OldestLaunchConfiguration, ClosestToNextInstanceHour, AllocationStrategy.

questions.question: What is an ASG Lifecycle Hook and when would you use it?
questions.answer: A Lifecycle Hook pauses an instance in a 'Wait' state during launch or termination, giving you time to perform custom actions before the transition completes. During Launch (Pending:Wait): run configuration scripts, register with service discovery, pull application code, validate instance. During Termination (Terminating:Wait): gracefully drain connections, deregister from service mesh, capture logs, backup state. Use cases: custom app initialization before receiving traffic, custom cleanup before shutdown. After your action completes, you send a 'CONTINUE' or 'ABANDON' signal to ASG. Default wait time is 1 hour.

questions.question: Explain how you would architect a highly available, auto-scaling web application on AWS from scratch.
questions.answer: Complete architecture: 1. VPC with public subnets (ALB) and private subnets (EC2) across 3 AZs. 2. Internet Gateway for public subnet. NAT Gateway for private subnet outbound. 3. ALB in public subnets, spanning all 3 AZs. ALB security group: inbound 80/443 from 0.0.0.0/0. 4. Target Group (EC2 type, HTTP:80, health check on /health). 5. ALB Listeners: port 80 redirect to 443; port 443 forward to Target Group (SSL certificate from ACM). 6. Launch Template: Amazon Linux 2, t3.medium, private security group (inbound HTTP from ALB SG only), user data to install and start app. 7. ASG: Minimum=3, Desired=3, Maximum=12. Subnets: all 3 private subnets. Attach to Target Group. ELB health checks enabled. Target Tracking: CPU 60%. 8. CloudWatch alarms for anomaly detection. SNS for alerts. Result: zero single points of failure, automatic traffic distribution, automatic scaling, instances never directly exposed to internet.
